title: HashiCorp Terraform Associate 003: The Certification That Proves You Can Build, Version, and Manage Infrastructure as Code
tldr: The HashiCorp Terraform Associate (003) is the standard IaC certification for DevOps, platform, and cloud engineers. 57 questions (multiple choice and multi-select), 60 minutes, approximately 70% to pass, $70.50 USD via PSI. Nine study objectives cover IaC concepts, HCL syntax, the core Terraform workflow (init → validate → plan → apply), state management, modules, and Terraform Cloud. No live terminal tasks — entirely theory and scenario-based. Version 003 replaced 002 in May 2023. Valid for two years.
bodyHtml:
What Terraform Associate 003 tests

The Terraform Associate is the foundational IaC certification for practitioners who provision and manage cloud infrastructure with Terraform. Version 003 (released May 2023) replaced 002 — updated Terraform Cloud content, Terraform 1.x semantics, and removal of deprecated 0.12 syntax. In August 2023, HashiCorp changed Terraform's licence to BSL; the OpenTofu fork emerged as the open-source continuation. The Terraform Associate 003 tests HashiCorp Terraform specifically. IBM acquired HashiCorp in 2024 — the certification programme continues unchanged.

Objective 1 — IaC Concepts

Terraform is declarative — describe desired end state, Terraform determines how to reach it. Idempotent by design. Mutable infrastructure is patched in place; immutable is replaced (new AMI or container image deployed, old instance terminated). Terraform enables the immutable model: most resource attribute changes trigger destroy-and-recreate. lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } controls replacement order. Terraform vs alternatives: CloudFormation (AWS-only, AWS-managed state, no multi-cloud), Ansible (configuration management, procedural, no lifecycle management), Pulumi (multi-cloud, general-purpose languages instead of HCL), Azure Bicep (Azure-only).

Objectives 2–3 — HCL Syntax and Terraform Basics

Block types: resource, data, variable, output, locals, module, terraform, provider. Primitive types: string, number, bool. Collection types: list(string), set(string), map(string). Structural: object({...}), tuple([...]). Meta-arguments: depends_on (explicit dependencies), count (N copies, differentiated by count.index), for_each (one per map key/set element — preferred over count for named resources), lifecycle (create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes, replace_triggered_by). Key functions: length(), element(), contains(), merge(), flatten(), toset(), lookup(map, key, default), format(), join(), cidrsubnet(), jsonencode(). Version constraints: ~> 4.0 (allows 4.x, not 5.0). The .terraform.lock.hcl file records exact provider versions — commit to source control.

Objective 4 — Core Terraform Workflow and CLI

Standard workflow: Write → init → validate → plan → apply. terraform init: downloads provider plugins, module sources, configures backend. terraform validate: checks syntax and semantics, no API calls. terraform plan: reads state, calls provider APIs, computes diff (+create, ~update, -/+replace, -destroy); use -out=plan.tfplan to save for deterministic apply. terraform apply: provisions resources, updates terraform.tfstate. terraform destroy: equivalent to terraform apply -destroy. Additional CLI: terraform fmt (auto-format), terraform show (print state or plan), terraform output (read outputs, -json for scripting), terraform console (interactive expression evaluator), terraform apply -replace=resource.type.name (force replacement, replaces deprecated taint), -target for scoped operations (avoid in routine production use).

Objective 7 — State Management

terraform.tfstate is a JSON file mapping configuration to real resources. Contains sensitive data — never commit unencrypted to source control. Remote backends: S3+DynamoDB (S3 stores state, DynamoDB provides locking via LockID attribute), Azure Blob Storage (built-in lease), GCS (object lock), Terraform Cloud (natively integrated, encrypted, versioned). State commands: terraform state list, terraform state show, terraform state mv (rename without reprovisioning), terraform state rm (remove from state without destroying), terraform import (bring existing resource under Terraform management). CLI workspaces (terraform workspace new) use different state files in the same backend — lightweight isolation for dev/staging/prod. Fundamentally different from Terraform Cloud workspaces.

Objective 5 — Modules

A module is any directory with .tf files. Root module = working directory. Child modules called via module blocks. Source types: local path (./modules/vpc — no versioning), Terraform Registry (hashicorp/consul/aws format, pin with version = ~> 0.0.5), private registry (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise), GitHub/Git (github.com/org/repo?ref=v1.2.0). Inputs via variable blocks in the module, outputs via output blocks — reference as module.name.output_name. Providers can be passed explicitly via the providers meta-argument for multi-account or multi-region patterns. Public Registry modules must follow terraform-PROVIDER-NAME naming and semantic versioning.

Objective 9 — Terraform Cloud

Terraform Cloud provides: remote state (encrypted, versioned, locked per run), remote runs (plan and apply on TFC-managed agents — no local credentials needed), VCS integration (plans triggered on pull requests), team RBAC (viewer/planner/operator per workspace), variable sets (reusable across workspaces), audit logging, Sentinel policy-as-code (paid tiers). Key concept: TFC workspaces are full environment representations with separate VCS connections, variable sets, state, and run histories — fundamentally different from CLI workspaces (terraform workspace new), which just use different state files in the same backend configuration.

Exam logistics and career impact

No prerequisites. $70.50 USD, online via PSI, 60 minutes, ~70% to pass, valid 2 years. HashiCorp recommends 6+ months of Terraform experience. Official study resources on developer.hashicorp.com: Terraform Associate Tutorial collection, Study Guide, and Sample Questions — all free. Bryan Krausen's practice exams on Udemy are the leading third-party resource. Typical prep: 4–6 weeks with hands-on labs covering the full workflow, module authoring, remote backend configuration, and Terraform Cloud. Salary: $120,000–$165,000+ for Terraform-certified platform/infrastructure engineers in major US markets (2025–2026). Appears alongside AWS SAA, CKA, and Azure Administrator on cloud infrastructure job postings.
